cues.text: Chapter three: IT infrastructure and agility.
Let us begin with a simple question.
When a business runs a digital service, such as a banking app, an online shop or a student portal, where does that service actually live, and what keeps it running?
The answer is infrastructure.
Infrastructure is the foundation beneath every digital service, and in this chapter we will see how the choices made at that foundation can either help an organisation adapt quickly or hold it back.
So, what does infrastructure include?
The source lists several things.
First, hardware, meaning the physical machines such as servers and devices.
Second, software, the programs that run on that hardware.
Third, networks, which connect machines and people together.
Fourth, storage, where data is kept.
Fifth, identity, which means the systems that establish who a user or a system is and what they are allowed to access.
Sixth, cloud services, which are computing resources delivered by a provider over a network.
And seventh, operational tools, the tools used to run, monitor and manage all of the above.
Notice that infrastructure is not only machines in a room.
It includes identity and operational tools, which means it covers how things are controlled and managed as well.
Now let us look at three ways of arranging this infrastructure, starting with on-premises infrastructure.
On-premises means the organisation owns and runs the infrastructure itself, in its own facilities.
The benefit, according to the source, is direct control.
You decide how things are configured and managed.
But that control has a price.
The organisation must do capacity planning, which means estimating in advance how much computing power, storage and network capacity it will need, and then providing it.
It must also handle maintenance, keeping the systems working and up to date.
If you guess too low, services struggle.
If you guess too high, you have paid for capacity you do not use.
The second arrangement is public cloud.
Here a provider supplies the resources.
The source says public cloud offers on-demand capacity and managed services.
On-demand capacity means you can obtain resources when you need them rather than buying them in advance.
Managed services means the provider takes on part of the operating work for you.
But the source is careful to state the trade-offs.
There are recurring costs, meaning you keep paying as you keep using the service, rather than paying mainly up front.
And there are network and provider dependencies.
Your service now relies on a network connection to the provider, and on the provider itself being available and suitable for your needs.
The third arrangement is hybrid cloud, which combines environments.
For example, an organisation might keep some systems in its own facilities and use a public cloud for others.
The source gives a clear warning here.
In a hybrid cloud, integration, access control and latency must be engineered.
Integration means making the different environments work together.
Access control means making sure the right people and systems have the right permissions across both.
Latency is the delay in communication between systems, and when parts of a service sit in different places, that delay matters.
The key word is engineered.
These do not take care of themselves.
They require deliberate design.
Now we turn to agility.
The source defines agility as the ability to adapt quickly and effectively to changing needs.
Pay attention to both words, quickly and effectively.
The source also makes two important clarifications.
Agility is not simply speed.
And it is not the absence of governance.
An organisation that moves fast and carelessly, or that drops its controls and oversight, is not agile.
It is just reckless.
Real agility means adapting well.
How do organisations become agile technically?
The source lists several enablers that can shorten feedback loops.
A feedback loop is the time between making a change and learning whether it worked.
The shorter that loop, the faster a team can learn and adjust.
The enablers are these.
Modular architecture, where a system is built from parts that can be changed separately.
APIs, which are defined ways for software components to communicate with one another.
Automated testing, where checks run automatically to confirm that changes have not broken anything.
Continuous integration, where code changes are combined and checked frequently.
Deployment automation, where releasing software is done by automated processes rather than by hand.
Observability, which is the ability to see what is happening inside running systems so that problems and behaviour can be understood.
And finally, skilled teams, because tools alone do not create agility.
People who know how to use them do.
The source then distinguishes some related practices.
Agile development delivers iterative increments.
That means work is delivered in repeated, small pieces rather than in one large release at the end.
DevOps improves collaboration and delivery and operations practices.
In other words, it brings together the people who build software and the people who run it, so that they work with shared practices rather than in separate silos.
Then there is infrastructure as code, which makes provisioning repeatable.
Provisioning means setting up the infrastructure.
When that setup is described in code, it can be run again and again with consistent results, rather than relying on manual steps that vary from one occasion to the next.
One more point from this block deserves emphasis.
Security and resilience should be built into delivery rather than attached at the end.
Resilience means the ability to keep working or recover when something goes wrong.
If these are treated as final add-ons, they are likely to be weak or to slow everything down late in the process.
Built in from the start, they become part of how the organisation delivers.
Finally, let us consider two ways to structure an application.
The first is the monolith.
A monolith deploys major application functionality together, as one unit.
The source notes that this can be efficient and simple for a smaller team.
There is less to coordinate, and that is a real advantage.
The second is microservices.
Microservices divide functionality into independently deployable services aligned to domains.
A domain here means an area of the business, for example payments or customer accounts.

The potential benefits, in the source's words, are improved autonomy, because teams can work on their own services, and targeted scaling, because you can increase capacity for just the part that needs it.
But there are costs.
Microservices introduce network failures, since services now talk to each other across a network that can fail.
They introduce consistency issues, meaning it can be harder to keep data and behaviour aligned across separate services.
And they bring operational overhead, which is the extra work of running many services instead of one.
So which should you choose?
The source says to choose according to workload, team structure and constraints.
There is no universal winner.
It depends on what the system must do, how the teams are organised, and what limits apply.
The source closes with a caution that connects back to transformation.
Moving a tightly coupled monolith to cloud without improving bottlenecks may not deliver meaningful transformation.
Tightly coupled means the parts depend heavily on one another, so they are hard to change independently.
If you simply relocate such a system to the cloud and leave those bottlenecks in place, you have changed where it runs, but not how well the organisation can adapt.
The lesson of this chapter is that agility comes from how systems, practices and teams are designed, not merely from where the infrastructure is hosted.
